01.note: The evil kingdom of Greece issued a decree against the Jews: no wood for the altar, no first fruits brought to Jerusalem, and guards posted on the roads to stop pilgrims. The worthy and sin-fearing people of that generation covered their baskets of first fruits with dried figs and carried a pestle on their shoulders. When the guards asked where they were going, they said they were off to make two cakes of pressed figs with the mortar down the road and the pestle they carried. Once past the guards, they decorated the baskets and brought them to Jerusalem.
01.why: The mishna lists families who brought wood to the Temple on set days, including 'those who deceived the authorities with a pestle' and 'those who packed dried figs'. The Sages ask who these were, and this account is the answer.

terms.meaning: The first ripe produce of the year, which the Torah commands farmers to bring to the Temple in Jerusalem as an offering.
The wood laid on the altar in the Temple to keep its fire burning for the offerings.
The three festivals (Passover, Shavuot and Sukkot) on which Jews traveled to the Temple in Jerusalem.

02.note: The kingdom of Greece forbade the Jews to bring wood for the altar and posted guards on the roads to stop pilgrims. The sin-fearing people of that generation took their pieces of wood, built them into ladders and carried them on their shoulders. When the guards asked where they were going, they said they were going to bring down doves from a dovecote down the road with the ladders. Once past the guards, they took the ladders apart and brought the wood up to Jerusalem.
02.why: The mishna names the descendants of Salmai of Netophat among the families who brought wood to the Temple; this account explains who they were, and the Gemara notes that the name Salmai hints at sulam, the word for ladder.

people.name: Salmai of Netophat
people.about: Ancestor of a family that brought wood to the Temple; his descendants are the ones who smuggled wood past the guards as ladders.

terms.meaning: A teaching of the early Sages that was not included in the Mishna, quoted by the Gemara as an authoritative source.
The wood laid on the altar in the Temple to keep its fire burning for the offerings.

03.note: Rav came to Babylonia and saw the people reciting hallel, the psalms of praise, on the New Moon. He thought to stop them, but when he saw that they were skipping portions of it, he concluded that they were keeping the custom of their forefathers. The Gemara adds a teaching: an individual should not begin hallel on the New Moon, but if he has begun, he should finish it.
03.why: Rava has just argued that hallel on the New Moon is a custom, not a Torah requirement, and Rabbi Yohanan's list of days for the full hallel leaves the New Moon out. Rav's reaction in Babylonia shows the same thing: the shortened recital marked it as a custom.

people.name: Rav
people.about: A Sage who came to Babylonia and saw the local practice of reciting hallel on the New Moon.

terms.meaning: A set of psalms of praise (Psalms 113-118) recited on festivals.
The first day of a Hebrew month, a minor holiday.
A teaching of the early Sages that was not included in the Mishna, quoted by the Gemara as an authoritative source.

04.note: When the wicked Turnus Rufus plowed the Sanctuary, a decree went out to execute Rabban Gamliel. A Roman officer came into the study hall and called out, 'The man with the nose is wanted,' and Rabban Gamliel heard and went into hiding. The officer then went to him in secret and asked: if I save you, will you bring me into the World-to-Come? Rabban Gamliel said yes and swore to it. The officer went up to a roof, fell and died; since the Romans cancelled a decree when one of its makers died, Rabban Gamliel was saved, and a Divine Voice declared the officer destined for the World-to-Come.
04.why: The mishna lists the calamities of the Ninth of Av, among them that the city was plowed. The Gemara quotes this account of the plowing of the Sanctuary to fill in that entry.

people.name: Turnus Rufus
people.about: The wicked Roman official who plowed the Sanctuary.

people.name: Rabban Gamliel
people.about: A leading Sage against whom a death decree was issued; he hid and was saved by the officer.

people.name: the Roman officer
people.about: An officer who warned Rabban Gamliel, then gave his own life to cancel the decree in exchange for a place in the World-to-Come.

terms.meaning: The life after this one, in which the righteous are rewarded.
A voice from heaven that announces God's judgment.
The inner building of the Temple in Jerusalem.

05.note: When the First Temple was being destroyed, groups of young priests gathered with the Temple keys in their hands and climbed to the roof of the Sanctuary. They said to God: since we did not merit to be faithful treasurers, let the keys be handed to You. They threw the keys upward, and something like the palm of a hand came out and caught them. Then the young priests jumped and fell into the fire.
05.why: The discussion is about the Ninth of Av, the date the mishna gives for the destruction of both Temples. This account of the First Temple's fall follows, and the Gemara reads Isaiah's lament about people on the rooftops as referring to these priests.

people.name: the young priests
people.about: Groups of young priests who held the Temple keys and threw themselves into the fire as the Temple burned.

terms.meaning: The inner building of the Temple in Jerusalem.
Those trusted with caring for the Temple and its property; the priests say they failed in that trust.

06.note: When Yonatan ben Uzziel wrote his Aramaic translation of the Prophets, the land of Israel quaked and a Divine Voice asked who had revealed God's secrets to mankind. Yonatan stood up and said it was he, and that he had done it not for his own honor or his family's, but for God's honor, so that disputes would not multiply among the Jewish people. He also wanted to translate the Writings, but a Divine Voice told him: 'It is enough for you.' The Gemara explains that the Writings contain the time of the Messiah's coming.
06.why: The Gemara has just reported who composed the Aramaic translations read in synagogues, Onkelos for the Torah and Yonatan ben Uzziel for the Prophets. This account continues the report of Yonatan's work, and the Gemara then asks why his translation shook the land when Onkelos's did not.

people.name: Yonatan ben Uzziel
people.about: The author of the Aramaic translation of the Prophets, who answers the Divine Voice.

people.name: God
people.about: Speaks through a Divine Voice, challenging Yonatan and then stopping him from translating the Writings.

terms.meaning: A voice from heaven that announces God's will.
The third part of the Hebrew Bible, after the Torah and the Prophets; it includes Psalms, Proverbs, Esther and Daniel.
Here, an Aramaic rendering of the Bible, read aloud in synagogues so people could understand the Hebrew text.

07.note: Rabbi Elazar reported in the name of Rabbi Hanina that Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi planted a sapling on Purim, bathed in Tzippori on the seventeenth of Tammuz when the market wagons were passing, and sought to abolish the fast of the Ninth of Av, and that the Sages did not agree with him. Rabbi Abba bar Zavda said to Rabbi Elazar that it had not happened that way. That year, he said, the Ninth of Av fell on Shabbat and was postponed to Sunday, and Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi said that since it had been pushed off, it should be pushed off altogether; the Rabbis did not agree with him. Rabbi Elazar applied to him the verse 'Two are better than one.'
07.why: The Gemara goes on to ask how Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi could plant on Purim, when work is forbidden then, and answers that he planted on the day that was not Purim where he lived. The planting raises the question of which towns keep Purim on the fourteenth and which on the fifteenth.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi
people.about: Called Rabbi; the Sage whose unusual acts on Purim, the seventeenth of Tammuz and the Ninth of Av are reported.

people.name: Rabbi Elazar
people.about: Reports the incidents in the name of Rabbi Hanina.

people.name: Rabbi Hanina
people.about: The Sage in whose name Rabbi Elazar reports the incidents.

people.name: Rabbi Abba bar Zavda
people.about: Corrects Rabbi Elazar's account of what Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi said about the Ninth of Av.

terms.meaning: A summer fast day marking the breach of Jerusalem's walls, three weeks before the Ninth of Av.
The fast day mourning the destruction of the Temples.
The holiday celebrating the rescue of the Jews in the book of Esther, kept on the fourteenth or fifteenth of Adar depending on the town.

08.note: On Purim, Rabbi Yehuda Nesia sent Rabbi Oshaya the leg of a calf and a jug of wine. Rabbi Oshaya sent back his thanks: 'You have fulfilled through us, our teacher, both sending portions one to another and gifts to the poor.'
08.why: Rav Yosef has just taught that the verse in Esther requires two portions to one person and gifts to the poor. Rabbi Oshaya's reply shows a single generous gift to a poor scholar counting for both mitzvot.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda Nesia
people.about: Sent a Purim gift of meat and wine to Rabbi Oshaya.

people.name: Rabbi Oshaya
people.about: Received the gift; the text says he was poor, so it counted as a gift to the poor as well.

terms.meaning: The Purim mitzva, from the book of Esther, of sending gifts of food to a friend.
The Purim mitzva of giving charity to poor people.
A calf of especially fine quality, here a choice cut of meat.

09.note: Rabba sent Marei bar Mar a Purim gift by the hand of Abaye: a sack of dates and a cup of roasted flour. Abaye said Marei would now quote the saying, 'Even if a farmer becomes king, the basket does not leave his neck.' Marei bar Mar sent back a sack of ginger and a cup of long peppers, and Abaye said Rabba would now say, 'I sent him sweet things and he sent me sharp ones.' Abaye later said that he left Rabba's house already full, but at Marei bar Mar's he was served sixty plates of sixty dishes, ate sixty portions, and still wanted to eat the plate after the last one, a pot roast.
09.why: The Gemara is discussing the Purim mitzva of sending portions of food to a friend; this exchange follows the gift of Rabbi Yehuda Nesia to Rabbi Oshaya as another example, and Abaye then draws two folk sayings from his meal.

people.name: Rabba
people.about: Sent a plain Purim gift to Marei bar Mar; the translation's note says he was poor.

people.name: Marei bar Mar
people.about: Received Rabba's gift and sent back a costlier one, then hosted Abaye lavishly.

people.name: Abaye
people.about: Rabba's nephew and student, who carried the gifts and comments on each one.

terms.meaning: Gifts of food sent to a friend on Purim, a mitzva from the book of Esther.

10.note: Rabba and Rabbi Zeira held a Purim feast together and became drunk. Rabba arose and slaughtered Rabbi Zeira. The next day Rabba prayed for mercy and brought him back to life. The following year Rabba invited him to hold the Purim feast together again, and Rabbi Zeira answered: 'Miracles do not happen every hour.'
10.why: Rava has just ruled that a person must drink on Purim until he cannot tell 'cursed is Haman' from 'blessed is Mordecai.' This story comes right after that ruling and shows how such drinking once ended.

people.name: Rabba
people.about: Held a Purim feast with Rabbi Zeira, killed him while drunk, and revived him through prayer.

people.name: Rabbi Zeira
people.about: Rabba's companion at the feast, who declined to come back the next year.

terms.meaning: The festive meal eaten on Purim day, one of the holiday's mitzvot.

11.note: King Ptolemy gathered seventy-two Elders, put each in a separate room without telling them why, and asked each to write him a translation of the Torah of Moses. God put wisdom in each one's heart, and all of them made the same changes to the text. They wrote, for example, 'God created in the beginning' rather than an order that could read as 'Bereshit created God,' and 'I shall make man' rather than 'Let us make man,' to avoid implying more than one power. They also changed verses that might shame Jacob's sons or Moses. For the hare they wrote 'the short-legged beast,' because Ptolemy's wife was named Arnevet, the Hebrew word for hare, and they did not want him to say the Jews had mocked him by putting her name in the Torah.
11.why: The discussion is about which languages a Torah scroll may be written in; Rabbi Yehuda says the Sages allowed Greek only for a Torah scroll. The Gemara gives the Ptolemy incident as the reason Greek was singled out.

people.name: King Ptolemy
people.about: King of Egypt, who had seventy-two Elders translate the Torah separately.

people.name: God
people.about: Put the same understanding in the heart of each Elder, so all their translations matched.

people.name: the seventy-two Elders
people.about: Sages of Israel who each translated the Torah alone and all made the same changes.

terms.meaning: A teaching of the early Sages that was not included in the Mishna, quoted by the Gemara as an authoritative source.
The Five Books of Moses, the first part of the Hebrew Bible.

12.note: A High Priest became temporarily disqualified, and the priest Rabbi Yosef ben Elem of Tzippori was appointed to serve in his place. When the disqualification passed, the case came before the Sages. They ruled that the original High Priest returns to his service, and the second is fit to serve neither as High Priest nor as an ordinary priest.
12.why: Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yosei disagree about a substitute High Priest once the original returns; Rabbi Yosei cites this case to back his view that the substitute may serve in neither role, and the Gemara gives the reasons: jealousy, and the rule that holiness is raised, never lowered.

people.name: Rabbi Yosei
people.about: The Sage who reports the incident.

people.name: Rabbi Yosef ben Elem of Tzippori
people.about: A priest appointed to stand in for a disqualified High Priest.

terms.meaning: The chief priest of the Temple, who alone performed certain services.
A temporary condition, such as ritual impurity, that kept the High Priest from serving.
An ordinary priest, below the High Priest.

13.note: Rabbi Abba compares Ahasuerus and Haman to two men: one had a mound of earth in the middle of his field, the other a ditch in his. The owner of the ditch wished he could buy the mound, and the owner of the mound wished he could buy the ditch. One day they met, and the ditch owner said, 'Sell me your mound.' The mound owner answered, 'Take it for free, and gladly.'
13.why: The Gemara is reading Esther verse by verse. Haman has offered the king ten thousand talents of silver, and the king answers, 'The silver is given to you, the people also.' Rabbi Abba's parable explains why the king took no money: he wanted the Jews destroyed just as much as Haman did.

people.name: Rabbi Abba
people.about: The Sage who tells the parable.

people.name: Ahasuerus
people.about: The Persian king of the book of Esther, compared to one of the two field owners.

people.name: Haman
people.about: The king's minister who wanted to destroy the Jews, compared to the other field owner.

terms.meaning: A short made-up story used to explain something by comparison.

14.note: The Sages did not know what several rare words meant, and learned them from everyday speech. They heard the maidservant in Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi's house ask Sages coming in a few at a time, 'How long will you come in seirugin seirugin?', and learned that seirugin means at intervals. They heard her use other words while talking to a man scattering purslane, to a man twirling his hair, and to a friend she told to sweep the house, and so learned the words for purslane, for turning something round, and for a broom. Rabba bar bar Hana told how an Arab he was traveling with said to him, 'Take your yehav and throw it on my camel,' and he understood that yehav means a load.
14.why: The mishna rules that one who reads the Megilla seirugin has fulfilled his obligation, and the Gemara needs to know what the word means. The maidservant's question explains it, and the other words follow as a chain of similar cases.

people.name: the maidservant in Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi's house
people.about: Her everyday Hebrew taught the Sages the meaning of several rare words.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi
people.about: Called Rabbi; the Sage whose household servant is overheard.

people.name: Rabba bar bar Hana
people.about: Learned the meaning of yehav from an Arab traveling companion.

terms.meaning: The scroll of the book of Esther, read aloud on Purim.
A leafy green plant that grows wild and is eaten as a vegetable.

15.note: Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar told of Rabbi Meir, who went to Asia Minor to fix the calendar by adding a month to the year. When Purim came there was no Megilla there, so he wrote one from memory and read from it.
15.why: Rabbi Yohanan has ruled that one may not write even a single letter of the Bible except by copying from a written text. The Gemara raises Rabbi Meir's Megilla as an objection, and answers that Rabbi Meir knew the text exactly and that an emergency is different.

people.name: Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar
people.about: Reports the incident.

people.name: Rabbi Meir
people.about: A Sage who wrote out a Megilla from memory when none could be found.

terms.meaning: The scroll of the book of Esther, read aloud on Purim.
To add an extra month to the Hebrew year to keep the calendar in step with the seasons, a decision made by the Sages.

16.note: Rav came to Babylonia on a public fast day and stood up to read from the Torah scroll. He said a blessing before he began reading, but none when he finished. Afterward everyone else fell on their faces in prayer, but Rav did not fall on his face.
16.why: The Gemara wants to know how many people read from the Torah on a public fast, three or four. It argues from Rav's missing closing blessing that someone read after him, which would make four, and then rejects the proof.

people.name: Rav
people.about: A leading Sage who read from the Torah on a fast day in Babylonia.

terms.meaning: A fast day declared for the whole community, for example in a drought.
Bowing down to the ground during a supplication prayer said after the main prayer.

17.note: Rav came to Babylonia on a public fast day and stood up to read from the Torah scroll. He said a blessing before he began reading, but none when he finished. Everyone else then fell on their faces in prayer, but Rav did not, and the Gemara asks why.
17.why: Having used this incident to count the Torah readers on a fast day, the Gemara now asks why Rav did not bow. It answers that the floor in front of him was stone, and the Torah forbids bowing on figured stone outside the Temple.

people.name: Rav
people.about: A leading Sage who read from the Torah on a fast day in Babylonia and did not bow with the rest.

terms.meaning: A fast day declared for the whole community, for example in a drought.
Bowing down to the ground during a supplication prayer said after the main prayer.

18.note: Levi demonstrated the bow called kidda in front of Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, and in doing it he became lame.
18.why: The Gemara has just defined three kinds of bowing, kidda among them. It then asks whether this caused Levi's limp, since Rabbi Elazar says Levi was lamed for speaking impertinently to God, and answers that both did.

people.name: Levi
people.about: A Sage who became lame while demonstrating a bow.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi
people.about: Called Rabbi; the Sage before whom Levi demonstrated the bow.

terms.meaning: A form of bowing with the face toward the ground; the translation's note describes the High Priest's version as bending from the waist until the head touches the ground.

19.note: Rabbi Yosei said that all his life he was troubled by the verse 'You shall grope at noon as the blind man gropes in the darkness': what difference does dark or light make to a blind man? Then one night, walking in total darkness, he met a blind man carrying a torch. He asked, 'My son, why do you need this torch?' The blind man answered: 'As long as I have a torch in my hand, people see me and save me from the pits and the thorns and the thistles.'
19.why: Rabbi Yehuda says a man who has never seen may not say the blessing over the heavenly lights, since he gets no benefit from them. The Rabbis disagree, and this story supplies their reason: a blind man benefits from light too.

people.name: Rabbi Yosei
people.about: A Sage puzzled by a verse until he met a blind man carrying a torch.

people.name: the blind man
people.about: Walking at night with a torch so that others could see him and keep him from harm.

terms.meaning: A teaching of the early Sages that was not included in the Mishna, quoted by the Gemara as an authoritative source.

20.note: A man led the prayers in front of Rabba and said: 'You had pity on the bird's nest, have pity and mercy on us; You had pity on an animal and its young, have pity and mercy on us.' Rabba said, 'How well this rabbi knows how to win his Master's favor!' Abaye said to him: 'But didn't we learn in the mishna that we silence him?'
20.why: The mishna says a prayer leader who mentions God's mercy on the bird's nest is silenced, and two Sages have just given reasons. The Gemara then explains that Rabba knew the rule and spoke only to sharpen Abaye's mind.

people.name: Rabba
people.about: A Sage who praised the prayer leader's words.

people.name: Abaye
people.about: Objects to Rabba that the mishna says such a prayer leader is silenced.

terms.meaning: The Torah's command to send away a mother bird before taking her eggs or chicks.
The Torah's ban on slaughtering an animal and its young on the same day.
The early collection of Jewish law on which the Gemara comments.
